cls: Vitamin D analogue (1-alpha-hydroxylated prodrug of calcitriol)
quick: 1 microgram once daily initially; titrate to calcium and PTH (typically 0.25-1 microgram/day)
With or without food; oral drops/capsules
Use only if clearly needed; avoid hypercalcemia
Preferred in renal failure (no renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation needed); watch calcium/phosphate
Requires hepatic 25-hydroxylation; effect may be altered in severe liver disease
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, renal function
summary: Alfacalcidol is a synthetic vitamin D analogue (1-alpha-hydroxyvitamin D3). Unlike native vitamin D, it requires only hepatic 25-hydroxylation - not renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation - to become active calcitriol, making it especially useful in renal failure where renal activation is impaired. It is used for renal osteodystrophy, hypoparathyroidism, hypophosphatemic/vitamin-D-dependent rickets, and other states of impaired vitamin D activation. Dosing is individualized to serum calcium and PTH; the main risk is hypercalcemia.
indications: Renal osteodystrophy / CKD-mineral and bone disorder
Vitamin D-dependent rickets and hypophosphatemic vitamin-D-resistant rickets

dosage.n: Titrate to serum calcium and PTH

admin: Take orally once daily (capsule or oral drops/solution); with or without food
Start low and titrate slowly based on serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH
Ensure adequate but not excessive dietary calcium; avoid additional high-dose vitamin D
Monitor serum calcium regularly during titration to avoid hypercalcemia
Correct hyperphosphatemia (e.g., with phosphate binders) before/while treating renal bone disease
moa: Alfacalcidol (1-alpha-hydroxyvitamin D3) is rapidly converted in the liver by 25-hydroxylase to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (calcitriol), the biologically active vitamin D hormone. Calcitriol binds the vitamin D receptor to increase intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, promote bone mineralization and remodeling, and suppress parathyroid hormone secretion. Because it bypasses the renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation step, it is effective even when renal activation of native vitamin D is impaired.

relative: Hyperphosphatemia (correct before treating renal bone disease)
Concurrent high-dose vitamin D, calcium, or thiazide diuretics
Sarcoidosis or other granulomatous disease (vitamin D hypersensitivity)

preg: Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed and at the lowest effective dose. Maternal hypercalcemia must be avoided as it can adversely affect the fetus. Monitor serum calcium closely.
lact: Vitamin D metabolites are excreted into breast milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding and monitor the infant for hypercalcemia, particularly if the mother is also taking vitamin D supplements.
renal: Particularly useful in renal failure because activation does not require renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase. Monitor serum calcium and phosphate closely; control hyperphosphatemia first to prevent metastatic calcification and aim to suppress secondary hyperparathyroidism without causing hypercalcemia or adynamic bone disease.
hepatic: Activation requires hepatic 25-hydroxylation; in severe hepatic impairment the conversion and clinical response may be altered. Monitor calcium and clinical response and adjust dose accordingly.

major: Other vitamin D preparations / calcitriol (additive risk of hypercalcemia and vitamin D toxicity)
moderate: Thiazide diuretics (reduce urinary calcium excretion - hypercalcemia risk)
Digoxin (hypercalcemia increases risk of digoxin toxicity/arrhythmia)
minor: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants/barbiturates (may increase metabolism, reducing effect)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum calcium and phosphate; alters PTH and alkaline phosphatase

common: Hypercalcemia (with nausea, constipation, thirst, polyuria, weakness)
emergency: Hypercalcemic crisis (severe dehydration, confusion, arrhythmia, coma)

monitoring: Serum calcium frequently during initiation and titration, then periodically
Renal function and urinary calcium where relevant
counsel: Take exactly the prescribed dose - too much can raise blood calcium dangerously
Keep all blood test appointments to monitor calcium and phosphate
Report nausea, vomiting, constipation, excessive thirst, frequent urination, or confusion
Do not take extra vitamin D or calcium supplements without medical advice
Maintain the recommended diet for your kidney/bone condition
pk: Rise in serum calcium typically within a few days; full effect over 1-2 weeks
Peak calcemic effect within several hours to days after conversion to calcitriol
Active calcitriol half-life approximately several hours; biologic calcemic effect persists days
Effects on calcium can persist for days after stopping (important for managing hypercalcemia)
Store below 25 C; protect from light; keep oily capsules/drops away from heat
pearls: Not a primary FDA-approved product in the US; widely used per EMA/SmPC and BNF (One-Alpha) - this record draws on those sources
Bypasses the renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation step, so it works in renal failure where calcitriol production is impaired
Hypercalcemia is the key dose-limiting toxicity - titrate to serum calcium and PTH
Effects persist for days after stopping; if hypercalcemia occurs, withhold the drug and recheck calcium before restarting at a lower dose
missed: If a dose is missed, take it when remembered the same day; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose. Do not double up - excess can raise blood calcium.
overdose: Overdose causes hypercalcemia (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, weakness, confusion) and potentially nephrocalcinosis and arrhythmia. Management: stop alfacalcidol and calcium/vitamin D intake, restrict dietary calcium, rehydrate (IV saine), and use loop diuretics; severe cases may need corticosteroids, calcitonin, or bisphosphonates. Effects can persist for days because of the active metabolite.
